content:
We’ve been doing computations with Real-valued functions using a type class-based approach (e.g.here and here and here). The paradigm is different from the more common interval arithmetic-based approaches, and I wanted to see what the community thinks about this overall approach. Essentially, this paradigm allows for verification of the logic of the functions, while simply accepting that they are implemented approximately by computers using Floats instead of true Reals. We don’t have experiments with efficiency, but I think our approach will beat interval arithmetic approaches in speed, since there’s just less to do on the computing side of things.

This is generally how those building physics / chemistry simulations see their code: a particle in space and time, a parcel of fluid, and a wavefunction all have various continuous properties that must be rounded off at some appropriate level of precision for computations to be possible. Sometimes, one is concerned about the round-off errors, but other times we're comfortable ignoring those, assuming they are much smaller than the deviation between experiments and the model. Our goal is to set up the derivations behind the functions using proofs over Reals, and then just substitute the Reals for Floats and compute after that.

In any case, after building different versions of this typeclass for a few different projects, I realized we could try to unify these, and define a single typeclass that would work for all of them. And then I started to wonder, could there be a “universal” RealLike typeclass that would flexibly handle Real->Float conversion across a broad range of applications? And then I started wondering if the Lean community (Would CSLib be interested? Would PhysLib be interested?) in collectively defining and maintaining such a thing (call it “RealLike” or maybe “ConvertToFloat” or something), thereby setting a standard for those in the community to use across multiple projects. It’s not obvious to me where the edge cases are, whether this would be of interest to others, and where it's home should be. For example, my student @Oscar Matemb ⚛️ is building a formally-verified implementation of the bisection method that imports RealLike, uses proofs about function continuity and root existence over Reals, and executes the bisection algorithm using Floats.

A separate question, is ``How seamless can we make execution of Real-valued functions?'' A pain point for us has been that, in building something that integrates all three types (alpha, Real, and Float), we end up writing Real-valued definitions and proofs in one stage, writing Float-valued functions in another stage, harmonizing them, then finally building the alpha-typed version of those. Wanting to get around this, we built a new command #evalf (meaning "#eval but with floats"). This is designed to feel like #eval in its usage, but allows certain kinds of noncomputable Real functions to be used in computations. See it in use here.

Our first prototype was a rather simple metaprogram that takes in a Real function, swaps out the Real types for Floats, and executes it - this actually went around the type class entirely, but worked very efficiently. But we quickly found this idea doesn't work compositionally, so we built a much, much larger metaprogram that does. This takes in a Real-valued function, then behind the scenes, it lowers it to the alpha type via the RealLike type class, and then specializes that to Float before executing. With evalf%, the Real-to-Float conversion machinery can be used in-line, for when you have a Float execution pipeline in which you want to use a Real-valued function.

We can also point #evalf at some Real-valued functions in PhysLib and seamlessly run computations on those, even when they're functions of types like Space and Time that themselves wrap around Reals, so one can have a function like noncomputable def timeShift (t : Time) : Time := t + 1 and use this directly in computations. I had originally envisioned this might enable computations for lots of noncomputable PhysLib functions, but that's not actually the case - we only around 30 or so functions with this version of #evalf, according to some code I had trying to survey this. I vibe-coded the #evalf command back in February, and I love the idea, though I do not vouch for this particular implementation, since I don't understand metaprogramming myself (the Lowering file itself grew to over 700 lines of code).

Anyways, we're eager for some feedback, especially on whether this sort of type class would be relevant for CSLib. There have been various approaches to handling computable Reals, and I'm curious about whether ours would be of broader interest.

Tyler Josephson ⚛️ said:

We’ve been doing computations with Real-valued functions using a type class-based approach (e.g.here and here)

These two links go to the same thing
I've created https://github.com/ATOMSLab/LeanLJ/pull/17 which removes a lot of the boilerplate of that code
I think @Tomas Skrivan had something similar for scilean.

@Eric Wieser Should definitely give you credit for this! We bundled our ad hoc instances together because of your idea and suggestion (RealLikeis the name we've stuck with, after all) (#general > Preprint: LeanLJ @ 💬 )

No need to give credit for what is essentially

class RealLike (α : Type) extends HasRound α, HasSqrt α,
    Add α, Sub α, Mul α, Div α, Neg α, Zero α, One α, NatCast α, IntCast α,
    Pow α ℕ, LE α, LT α where
  [decidableLE : DecidableLE α]
  [decidableLT : DecidableLT α]

I think when we wrote the LeanLJ paper, there wasn't a HasRound or HasSqrt, so we had to build it less elegantly. Thanks for the PR, but we aren't maintaining that repo anymore. I think for the LeanBET and RealLike repos, we could use this to clean those up.

But my main questions are - could/should a RealLike typeclass be constructed that subsumed ... all of a handheld calculator's functions? More? What should it include? Would it be nice to centralize and maintain something like this in one of the libraries?
I don't think it's reasonable to create "one class to rule them all"; but we could certainly consider creating something like RingOps which is Ring without any of the proofs, etc

I have bunch of different versions of RealLike floating around my repositories but I have never figured out what should be the canonical definition. What do you do about all the transcendental functions?

  1. Do you add them as parts of the class?
  2. Do you make a class for each transcendental function?

Problem with 1. there will be always some transcendental function missing 2. How do you avoid your functions to have type signatures likefoo {R} [RealOps R] [HasSine R] [HasCos R] [HasExp R] ... [HasGammaFunction R] ...

With option 2., do you need a lot of typeclasses for a single function? If it's RingOps + 2 or 3 HasFun typeclasses it's not so bad. The algorithms I have in mind each need a few (say sqrt and log, for one of the algorithms in the Lean Machine Learning repo), but not many.

I think it's possible to keep adding more transcendental functions until none are missing. I can imagine this list getting longer. And then, if someone thinks of one that's missing, it can be added to the "one class to rule them all" if we think it's common enough, or they can extend the class themselves if they want to. I wonder about efficiency tradeoffs, perhaps, but I think a list of "calculator-like" functions is a reasonable place to start.

But I'm more concerned about legimate conflicts - I haven't thought of any edge cases, but would there but something where there wouldn't be one "right way" to link a Real operation with a Float operation?

Yes both counter points are absolutely valid

  1. There is a reasonable finite set of functions that one might want to use
  2. Yes usually there is only very few functions used so it is not such an issue. Also considering you can just write variable {R} [RealLike R] [HasSin R] ... [HasLog R] ... at the top of your file and just forget about this issue.

Tyler Josephson ⚛️ said:

and here

I had a quick look at this project; is there a reason you are not setting these up with lake new RealLike math, which would configure the .gitignore and CI?
That would also be a useful API for continued fractions, continued logarithms, and other stream representations! (ignoring computability of HasRound, LE, etc.)

I in principle really like this idea. If the plan is to only ever use the float version for evaluation, I can imagine another system (which likely has its own advantages and disadvantages) , which is just based on meta-programming.

The system I have in mind is to have an attribute like @[FloatEquivalent ...] which can be applied to definition e.g. 

@[FloatEquivalent Float]
def Real : Type :=....

@[FloatEquivalent Float.sin]
def Real.sin : Real -> Real := ....

Then if you take an arbitrary function e.g. f : Real x Real -> Real, if it is possible to reduce the syntax tree enough a simple substitution from Real to the FloatEquivalent should be possible (taking care of the bounded and free variables). This could be done automatically whenever you call e.g. #evalf f (...).

Not sure if this would have different features, but I think it would get around @Tomas Skrivan 's second point of needing a typeclass for every type of function.

This meta programming approach is also something I have explored a bit. I wrote a meta program that runs simp on your program before compiling and allows you to also define type encodings that can swap one type for another. For example, you can say that Real should be encoded as Float and then define bunch of simp theorems saying how to translate operations on reals to operations on floats. For example

@[sas_encoding]
theorem add (x y : Real) : (x + y) = decode (encode x + encode y) := sorry

where encode : Float -> Real and decode : Real -> Float. Of course this theorem is false, I'm just using Lean's theorems as a database for registering compiler rewrites.

The meta program takes function 

def foo (x : Real) := exp (x + x) + sin (x * x)

rewrites it as

def foo._spec (x : Float) : Float := encode (exp (decode x + decode x) + sin (decode x * decode x))

and runs simp its body with all the theorems marked with sas_encoding The simp will hopefully removing all operations on Real and produce computable function.

The nice thing is that you can reuse lots of Leans mechanisms. For example the type encoding is managed through the class TypeEncoding A B which will replace type A with B. So you can for example provide instance TypeEncoding A A' → TypeEncoding B B' → TypeEncoding (A×B) (A'×B') and get types like Real × Nat compiled to Float × Nat. The hope is that this will also allow to convert Fin n → ℝ to Vector Float n but I havn't done extensive testing of it yet.

Here is a test file demonstrating simple Real -> Float translation.

@Joseph Tooby-Smith This attribute idea sounds pretty neat. So, instead of storing “which Float function aligns with which Real function” in a centralized type class instance, one does this in a distributed way with attributes? One could also use FloatEquivalent for Rationals, too, to get a decimal approximation instead of a precise fraction. Traversing the syntax tree seems like a nice way to handle composition.

@Tomas Skrivan how does your approach handle composition? I don’t quite see it, but I see it in action with the main function. Neat idea to commandeer simp!

I think trying different implementations will be helpful, to compare compilation and execution speed. In our approach, execution via the RealLike typeclass is pretty fast, but execution of Real functions via #evalf is much, much slower.
In my approach, something like Real.sin (Real.exp x) gets translated to decode (Float.sin (encode (decode (Float.exp (encode x))))) then the inner encode (decode dissapears.
